newsitem.title: USA: MEAG revenue bonds rated A-minus - S&P.
newsitem.headline: MEAG revenue bonds rated A-minus - S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 17 - Standard & Poor's Corp Tuesday said
it has assigned its single-A'-minus rating to the Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia's $194.47 million subordinate revenue bonds (project 1) series 1996A.
The authority currently has about $3.7 billion in total debt outstanding.
Additionally, Standard & Poor's has affirmed its ratings on the authority as follows:
-- $2.28 billion senior lien power revenue bonds (project 1) at single- A', and
-- $888 million senior lien general resolution bonds (project 2, 3, and 4) at single-A'.

The ratings on the Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia's debt and its business position of somewhat below average' reflect the pressure on participants to maintain competitive retail rates in a deregulating environment, and the continuing problems the authority faces involving excess baseload capacity, which has contributed to sensitivity between the participants over the allocation of costs. The rating is supported by the following:
-- The strong legal protection provided by the court validated power sales contracts,
-- Regionally competitive wholesale cost of power to participants, and
-- The vibrant state economy, ranking in the top five states for employment and population growth.

Currently, the authority's cost of power to participants (5.18 cents per kWh in 1995) is about 7% lower than that of Oglethorpe Power Corp. (OPC) and about level with that of Georgia Power Co. (GPC), whose costs are projected to increase. OPC and GPC are the authority's two primary competitors for new loads. Current forecasts indicate that the authority's costs will hold steady at 5.06 cents per kWh through 2000. However, the authority's high fixed costs associated with its base load generation and expectations of declining wholesale power costs in the region, will present some challenge for the authority to continue to provide competitively priced power to its participants. At the retail level, the authority's participants rates, while generally competitive in the residential sector, are somewhat less competitive in the industrial sector. The average retail industrial rate for the authority's participants it 5.38 cents per kW as compared to 4.57 cents for the state. The authority invested in 1,558 MW of baseload nuclear (52%) and coal (48%) capacity. Each of the participants has been allocated a share of the capacity and makes payments to the authority based on this share through power sales contracts, which have been validated by the Georgia courts.

The participants' load growth has been slower than originally anticipated, leaving some participants with excess capacity. The costs associated with the excess capacity have been partially absorbed by participants, which are not overinvested.

Currently the authority is involved in litigation with one of its participants, Calhoun, over a dispute involving the pricing of supplemental power, the costs of which blend in part of the costs of the excess. The 1997 budget will provide for a fixed allocation of all fixed costs to the participants. Previously, fixed costs associated with projects # 2 and 3 (about 30% of total), had been blended with some of the cost of excess project one power. Supplemental power will be priced at market rates, and additional incentive rates will be provided for economic development and load retention. While this will result in some increase for those participants with excess capacity, the authority will take steps to minimize this, including the potential use of part of the about $200 million in rate stabilization funds.

The outlook reflects expectations that the authority management will be both proactive and successful in its efforts to provide competitively priced power, particularly given the potential for declining wholesale power costs. Standard & Poor's anticipates some stabilization or strengthening of participant relations, Standard & Poor's said.
